extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne; readers interested in moral philosophy and essays
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of Montaigne's essay on ignorance, simplicity, and the limits of human knowledge; the page argues norms for prudence, the value/risks of ignorance, and skeptical suspension of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive vivacity and pursuit of learning can ruin great wits
rubrics_metrics.description: Great wits are ruined by their own proper force and pliability; the vivacity that drives curiosity, exact apprehension, and laborious search after sciences can destroy judgement and impair life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an Italian poet reduced to imbecility by his vivacity; cautionary tone that forceful intellectual activity may lead to mental ruin rather than improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity/ignorance promotes steadiness and wellbeing
rubrics_metrics.description: If you would have a man healthy, regular, and secure, muffle him up in the shades of stupidity and sloth — simplicity leads to freedom from evils and a more contented life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-off acknowledged: dullness reduces sensitivity to both pain and pleasure; Montaigne argues the human condition values avoiding evils over attaining peak pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human beings feel pain more acutely than pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: We are not so sensible of the most perfect health as we are of the least sickness; the extremest pleasure does not affect us to the degree that a light grief does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported with classical quotations (Ennius) and the observation that the appetite for pleasure often seeks merely to remove discomfort rather than produce lasting positive sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total insensibility is undesirable and inhuman
rubrics_metrics.description: An insensibility that eliminates knowledge of evil would at the same time eradicate sense of pleasure and annihilate man; one ought not to aim for absolute insensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crantor's objection to Epicurus is cited: one should feel when sick or injured; complete obliviousness to pain is impractical and morally problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical palliatives (recalling pleasures) are limited or counterproductive
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy's counsel to divert thoughts from present ills by recalling past pleasures often fails and can even worsen suffering—'The thinking of pleasure doubles trouble.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes the prescription to dwell on past delights as a remedy for present pain and notes that memory does not obey our will in the way philosophers assume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory cannot be reliably controlled; forgetting is not voluntary
rubrics_metrics.description: To empty and disfurnish the memory is not within our power: 'I do also remember what I would not; but I cannot forget what I would.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects philosophical counsel that recommends willful oblivion; treating memory as controllable is naive and may lead to ignorance rather than wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: When cure fails, palliative comforts and 'frivolous appearances' are permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where philosophy cannot cure the wound, it is content to palliate and benumb it; borrowing frivolous appearances that administer satisfaction is allowed when force fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne concedes that safe, comforting illusions or habits may be preferable to relentless truth-seeking when they preserve order, constancy, or happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some prefer agreeable delusion to sober truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases of men (e.g., Lycas, Thrasylaus) show that being in a pleasant imaginary state can be more desirable than restored 'health' of mind; cured patients sometimes beg to be returned to their pleasing error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as evidence that ignorance or illusion can be a legitimate strategy for personal tranquillity; Montaigne treats such choices with ambivalence but understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide may be considered a last remedy when life is unbearable
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy admits putting an end to life which one is not able to endure; several philosophers historically chose death when learning or life became intolerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recounts examples (Sextius, Democritus) and cites the law's view that escape by death can be rational in extreme cases — presented descriptively rather than prescriptively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride and the thirst for knowledge are original sources of human ruin
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian interpretation: the thirst of knowledge and desire to be wiser was the first ruin of man; pride diverts man from common paths and leads to novelty and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne references scripture and Christian teaching to argue that intellectual ambition can foster presumption and heresy, so humility is a moral safeguard.

rubrics_metrics.name: True wisdom includes recognition of one's own ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: The wisest man is he who knows that he knows nothing; self-knowledge of ignorance is a mark of superior judgment and leads to modesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Socrates and other sages: acknowledging limits of knowledge tempers dogmatism and prevents pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pyrrhonian suspension of judgment (ataraxy) as a method for tranquility
rubrics_metrics.description: Pyrrhonists suspend assent — they debate, examine, and argue without fixing belief; this suspension produces ataraxy (peace), freeing them from anxieties born of opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes Pyrrhonian techniques: arguing both pro and con, refusing to commit, using equal appearances to avoid assent; in action they follow probable appearances and customs while withholding judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical life proceeds by appearances and customs despite philosophical doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: Even those who suspend judgment in theory conduct their lives by following laws, conventions, probable signs, and experience; doubt does not prevent ordinary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes skeptics rely on practical probabilities (e.g., seaworthiness, pilot's skill) and accept arts guided more by conjecture than dogmatic knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility before divine mysteries: some truths are better believed than known
rubrics_metrics.description: Divine matters are more properly met with belief than with human inquiry; 'God is better known by not knowing him' — revelation and faith benefit from human ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References St. Augustine, Tacitus, and Plato to argue that attempting to comprehensively explain the divine is impious; a 'blank paper' of humility better receives divine instruction.
